0.title: Four Switches, One Mechanism: What Stem Geometry Actually Changes
0.lede: The Durock T1, the Boba U4T, the Holy Panda X, and the Gateron Lanes have spent four separate deep-dives citing each other as comparison points. None of those pieces stopped to say the obvious thing: all four generate their bump the same way. The leg geometry is the whole story.

1.title: Artisan keycaps: a practical buying guide
1.lede: A single sculpted cap on the Escape key can cost more than the switches underneath it, and the buying process looks nothing like ordering a keycap set. Here is what an artisan actually is, how the raffles work, and the one check that keeps a buyer from winning a cap their board can't use.

2.title: GMK CYL Zombie's group buy, open through October 31, is already thock's steepest Halloween climb
2.lede: GMK CYL Zombie, a Halloween-themed colorway running jointly through KBDfans and KeyAtlas from October 2 through October 31, 2026, has climbed to a score of 70 on thock's 2026-W42 trends tracker off an eight-week spark trail that hasn't flattened once. The buy is roughly a third of the way through its run, not winding down.

3.title: Build of the week: the Drop CTRL goes synthwave under GMK Laser and Ink V2 Yellow
3.lede: A board tuned for directness, a switch tuned for speed, and a keycap set tuned for attention — the gap between the first two and the third is the entire reason this build works.

4.title: What a switch's gram number actually tells you before you buy
4.lede: Every switch spec sheet carries two gram numbers — actuation and bottom-out — and treating them as one number is the most common mistake in a first switch purchase. Here's what each one measures, what ranges actually suit typing versus gaming, and why the same number can feel completely different depending on switch type.

5.title: TMR is closing the gap on Hall-effect. It hasn't caught it.
5.lede: TMR switches have climbed every week on thock's trend tracker from W38 through W42 — 55, 63, 71, 85, 90. That's the second-highest score on this week's board, and the gap behind Hall-effect's ceiling has gone from 42 points to 10 in five readings.

6.title: What a TMR sensor is actually measuring under a magnetic switch
6.lede: Keychron's Q16 HE 8K and Cherry's XTRFY TMR boards get covered as a new switch generation. The real change sits a few millimeters below the magnet — a tunnel junction reading field strength through resistance instead of voltage, with a noise floor low enough to matter at the shallow end of the stroke.

7.title: Build of the week: the Bakeneko65 stops being a budget board under GMK Bentō R2 and Tecsee Sapphire V2
7.lede: A $150 evergreen hotswap board, a sold-out doubleshot ABS set, and a sparkly polycarbonate tactile aren't a mismatch — the cheap part of this build is the entry price, not the result.

8.title: Hardware caught up to Wooting. Firmware hasn't.
8.lede: Wooting's 80HE+ preorder is the top mover on thock's 2026-W39 trends tracker, climbing from a score of 40 to 80 over eight weeks. The switch hardware behind it isn't the reason — Hall-effect sensing is table stakes across the category by September 2026. The firmware behind it still isn't matched.

9.title: Wooting's 80HE+ preorder starts shipping in two waves this fall
9.lede: Preorders for Wooting's 80HE+ opened September 17, 2026, and the first units are headed out the door in two separate waves — ABS and Module boards in late October, the zinc case and Lekker Knob Large accessory in mid-December.

10.title: PCB flex cuts, explained: a flex budget milled straight into the board
10.lede: No plate change, no gasket, no case redesign — just a slot routed through the fiberglass near a switch hole. Flex cuts are the cheapest lever a designer has for adding give to a board that otherwise has none, and the cheapness is exactly why they show up where they do.

11.title: Wireless keyboard buying guide: Bluetooth, 2.4GHz, and the latency that actually matters
11.lede: "Wireless" on a spec sheet hides three different radios with three different latency numbers, battery habits, and ways to lose the thing. Here's how to pick the one that matches an actual desk instead of a marketing slide.

12.title: GMK CYL Red Devils is back after six years — and it's climbing the tracker faster than most first runs
12.lede: GMK CYL Red Devils returns after six years for a second run, open Sept 14–Oct 10, 2026 via Omnitype and Keebz N Cables. The thock trends tracker has it up to a score of 68 off one of the steepest eight-week climbs of the season — and the buyer base behind that climb looks nothing like the one that bought the original.

13.title: Keychron launches Q16 HE 8K with ceramic-TMR magnetic switches
13.lede: Keychron's Q-series just picked up a Kickstarter campaign, a ceramic-housed TMR magnetic switch, and an 8000Hz polling claim in one launch. It's the brand's first bet on tunnel-magnetoresistance sensing rather than the Hall-effect tech it already made the category default.

14.title: Build of the week: the mission control desk, in Class80, Godspeed, and Box White
14.lede: A retro TKL, a steel-blue-and-cream SA set, and a clicky box-stem switch aren't three separate purchases here — they're one decision, made three times, that only works because each part solves a problem the other two create.

15.title: How to clean and maintain a mechanical keyboard
15.lede: Dust, oil, and crumbs collect on every keyboard whether anyone notices or not. A light routine on a fixed cadence keeps a board feeling and sounding like day one — no teardown required.

16.title: Rapid trigger is a firmware algorithm, not a switch spec
16.lede: A rapid-trigger switch is not a special switch. It is an ordinary analog sensor wired to a polling loop that redraws its own actuation point every cycle — and that loop, not the sensor, is where the real engineering happens.

17.title: Cherry's tracker slide continues. Keychron's Kickstarter delivered.
17.lede: Three weeks ago thock closed a piece with two open questions: would Cherry's brand line keep closing the gap toward positive territory, and would Keychron's V6 Ultra HE Kickstarter give the tracker something new to climb on. Both questions have answers now, and they point in opposite directions for a related reason.

18.title: Drop restocks /dev/tty, the 2017 set that built the MT3 profile
18.lede: Drop's catalog listing for Matt3o's original MT3 /dev/tty set flipped to in-stock in late August 2026, returning the dye-sub PBT run that defined the profile.

19.title: Parts pairing for a split build: two independent halves, two independent decisions
19.lede: A split board is two keyboards that happen to share a keymap. Most builders still buy parts for it like it's one — matching switches, ordering a single sculpted keycap set, and never touching the left half's tuning differently from the right's.

20.title: Keyboard layout sizes, compared: 60% to full-size, which fits your desk
20.lede: 60%, 65%, 75%, TKL, full-size — the names read like a settled taxonomy, but each cut trades away a specific cluster of keys for a specific amount of desk space. Here's what a reader actually keeps and gives up at each size, and how a firmware layer changes the math.

21.title: Gateron Magnetic Jade: the Hall-effect linear built to be argued about like a mechanical one
21.lede: Pull a Magnetic Jade apart and the parts list reads like a mid-tier mechanical linear: polycarbonate top, nylon bottom, POM stem, factory lube. Where the leaf would be, there is a magnet. That one substitution explains the feel, the sound, and why it will not fit half the Hall-effect boards on the market.

22.title: What a silent switch actually silences — and what it can't
22.lede: Every keystroke lands twice — once on the floor, once on the ceiling. Cherry molds an elastomer pad onto the stem to catch both; Gazzew fits a silicone one. The undamped Boba U4T shows what either approach is buying — about 14 dB on one tester's meter — and what it costs in travel, rebound, and a bump with nowhere left to go.

23.title: Why stabilizers rattle: the engineering behind a smooth stab
23.lede: A stabilizer has to be loose enough to slide and tight enough to stay quiet, and those two requirements contradict each other at three separate interfaces. Every rattle, tick, and clunk on a spacebar is one of those interfaces losing the argument.

24.title: ANSI, ISO, or JIS: a practical layout buying guide
24.lede: Two boards can look nearly identical in a listing photo and still take entirely different keycap sets. Here's how to read Enter key shape, bottom-row widths, and spec-sheet shorthand before ordering — not after a set arrives that doesn't fit.

25.title: GMK CYL Orange Alert opens at Divinikey, the second Alert-series set to reach group buy this year
25.lede: GMK CYL Orange Alert opened August 14 and runs through September 14, 2026, hosted by Divinikey with KBDfans, UniKeys, and Keebz N Cables running alongside — an orange-beige-gray Cherry-profile doubleshot set with Katakana accent legends and an estimated February 2027 ship.

26.title: Hall-effect stopped climbing. That's not the same as cooling off.
26.lede: The Hall Effect/Rapid Trigger category has held flat at 97 on thock's trends tracker for two straight weeks, after climbing from 82 in late June. A flat line at the top of the chart looks like fading interest if you're reading it as a stock ticker. Read as a market snapshot, it says something closer to the opposite.

27.title: Hot-swap sockets: what you actually give up for the convenience
27.lede: Tool-free switch swapping turned hot-swap PCBs into the default spec across the hobby, and the default is earned. Here is the honest, specific list of what a socket costs against a soldered joint — and the two cases where soldering is still the right call.

28.title: Wuque Studio's summer update, and the Ikki68 Aurora holdover
28.lede: A July 26 product-update post from Wuque Studio sent buyers back to the Ikki68 Aurora's listing page. Mammoth V2 and Promise V2 remain forum speculation, and no group buy has opened.

29.title: How keycaps are actually made: double-shot, dye-sub, and the processes in between
29.lede: Material and profile get the attention. The mold, the second shot, the transfer press, and the shrinkage table are what set the price, the lead time, and whether the legend is still there in ten years.

30.title: GMK Just Beachy's group buy opens August 18 across five vendors on five regions
30.lede: GMK Just Beachy opens for orders August 18, 2026 at five vendors spanning five regions at once — Keebz N Cables, Divinikey, Prototypist, KBDfans, and Unikeys — capping an eight-week climb on thock's Trends Tracker that hasn't logged a single down week.

31.title: Leaf-spring mounts, explained: what a bending metal tab does that a foam strip cannot
31.lede: The Nyawice's spec line and Mode's plate-tab mounting blocks both lean on one old idea — let a thin tab bend instead of a foam strip squash. The physics is textbook; the keyboard implementations are not, and the name covers more than one mechanism.

32.title: GMK CYL TA Neo's group buy is closed — here's what a November 2026 ship estimate actually means
32.lede: GMK CYL TA Neo closed its group buy July 17, 2026 after a June 19 open, and the thock trends tracker has logged two straight weeks of cooling attention since. That's not a warning sign — it's what every closed keycap buy looks like while it waits on production.

33.title: What a split keyboard actually changes: the mechanics
33.lede: A conventional keyboard bends the wrist three separate ways, and every ergonomic geometry on the market is a fix for exactly one of them. Sorting out which fix does what — and which claims the research backs — is the difference between buying a posture and buying a story.

34.title: The Holee mod: what foam inside the switch actually buys you
34.lede: Small pads of polyurethane foam cut and wedged inside the switch housing itself — not under the PCB, not behind it, not under the keycap. The Holee mod works at a smaller scale than every other foam mod in the hobby, and it costs proportionally more time.

35.title: How the 60% became the default custom-keyboard layout
35.lede: Every custom-keyboard buyer's guide since the mid-2010s opens with the same four-term vocabulary — 60%, 65%, 75%, TKL — as though it always existed. It didn't. One open-source PCB out of a geekhack thread is most of the reason that taxonomy exists at all.

36.title: The Boba Family: One Housing Blend, Five Switches, and the Sound thock Is Named For
36.lede: Gazzew designs, Outemu molds, and a plastic softer than nylon does the rest. Every Boba is the same chamber with something deliberately left out — and the pattern of subtractions is the whole family tree.

37.title: How buckling-spring switches actually work
37.lede: thock has already reached for the buckling-spring snap twice — once to describe a Topre dome, once to describe a click-bar's sharpness — without ever explaining what a buckling spring actually is. The mechanism predates both, and it is stranger and more mechanically honest than either.

38.title: ZMK for wireless and split builds: a practical guide
38.lede: QMK answers almost every firmware question on a wired board. Add a battery and a second half, and the honest answer changes — this is the guide for the builder standing at that fork.

39.title: Mixing keycap profiles on one board: what actually works
39.lede: Mixing profiles reads as a deliberate design choice or a rookie mistake depending entirely on where the swap lands. A handful of zones tolerate it well. The alpha block almost never does.

40.title: Prototypist and the multi-project vendor model
40.lede: Prototypist rarely carries just one thing at a time. The UK vendor's tracker signal has spent 2026 rising and falling with how many group buys it's running at once — and in July 2026 it's climbing again on the strength of its own pipeline rather than someone else's.

41.title: Keyboard cables, compared: coiled, straight, and the connector that actually matters
41.lede: Every builder eventually stares at a cable dropdown and has to decide whether to care. Here's what coiled versus straight actually changes, and why the keyboard-side connector — not the color of the sleeve — is the decision that follows the board for its whole life.

42.title: OpenAI's first hardware is a Work Louder macro pad
42.lede: Codex Micro, OpenAI's first piece of branded hardware, is a macro pad built by boutique vendor Work Louder on the bones of its $199 Creator Micro 2. It launched July 15, 2026 at $230, sold out within 24 hours, and now resells for $700-800+.

43.title: Cherry bets on magnetic: the XTRFY pivot
43.lede: Cherry's mainline MX switches have spent the better part of a year losing ground on the tracker. On July 3, 2026, Cherry's gaming sub-brand XTRFY answered not with another MX revision but with a magnetic-sensing switch — and gave the parent brand its first positive tracker signal in months.

44.title: The Blaine V2: SE puts three mount systems in one kit and asks the buyer to pick
44.lede: CannonKeys's F12 TKL follow-up ships with top mount, single-sided gasket, and o-ring hardware in the same box, plus a carbon-fiber bottom plate and a POM underside element it calls Volcano. The mount menu is the story.

45.title: Nova Socket: Keychron's bet on not choosing a switch technology
45.lede: A single hot-swap socket that accepts a standard mechanical switch or a TMR magnetic switch, decided per key, is a strange thing for a mainstream prebuilt brand to ship. It's also exactly the move Keychron has been building toward all year.

46.title: The brass weight mod: what added mass actually buys you
46.lede: Bolting a half-pound of brass into the bottom of a case is one of the more expensive mods in the hobby for how little it visibly does. It changes how a board sounds and sits on a desk — just not in the ways the marketing copy implies.

47.title: Why the Durock T1's Bump Feels the Way It Does
47.lede: The Durock T1 keeps turning up as the comparison point in other switches' deep-dives — the reference a reviewer reaches for when a bump needs to read as heavy and serious. It has never had its own.

48.title: Why the Gazzew Boba U4T Rings Where the Boba U4 Stays Quiet
48.lede: Same housing, same bump position — the U4T's whole personality comes down to what Gazzew left out. Pull the dampening pads from a Boba U4 and the bottom-out stops being polite.

49.title: Choosing your first custom keyboard kit: a buyer's guide
49.lede: Most first custom keyboards aren't built from loose parts and aren't bought finished — they're a barebones kit, a case-plate-PCB bundle that leaves the rest of the decision to the buyer. Here's how to make that decision without guessing.

50.title: GMK CYL OG Extensions climbed eight interest-check weeks, then opened a group buy of its own
50.lede: An interest check posted on Geekhack pulled ahead of both open GMK CYL group buys on the thock trends tracker — eight straight weekly reads without a single flat week — before opening a group buy of its own that has kept climbing since.

51.title: Retrobrighting: what UV and peroxide actually reverse in yellowed ABS
51.lede: Vintage ABS keycaps go the color of weak tea, and the hobby's fix is a jar of hair developer and a sunny windowsill. The chemistry behind that fix is real — but it reverses one specific kind of damage, and builders regularly aim it at problems it cannot touch.

52.title: GMK CYL Masterpiece R2 closed at KBDfans, finishing the Katakana argument R1 started
52.lede: Energieschleuder's six-year-later return to Japanese craftsmanship aesthetics climbed the thock tracker all window, scoring 46 in W26 before the buy closed June 26.

53.title: GMK CYL Pandemonium: the eclipse-themed keycap set that closed on a plateau
53.lede: DeltaKeyCo's Berserk eclipse group buy climbed the tracker from its June 1 open, posting a score of 33 in W26 with a flat direction — a mid-window plateau it held through its July 1 close.

54.title: Split and ergonomic keyboards: a buyer's guide
54.lede: Split doesn't automatically mean ergonomic, and ergonomic doesn't automatically mean split. Before spending money on either, a reader needs to know which of four separate design choices they're actually buying — and which one of them is solving their problem.

55.title: Gateron Lanes: The Alps-Inspired Tactile Taking Over the Mid-Range
55.lede: Gateron's Lanes draws its DNA from the Alps SKCM Orange — one of the most loved tactile mechanisms of the 1980s — and arrived in June 2026 with enough community conviction to sell out on first drop.

56.title: Keychron's Quiet Takeover: How One Brand Became the Mechanical Keyboard Default
56.lede: Ask almost anyone — a forum regular, a YouTube comment section, a Discord server for people who just bought their first mechanical keyboard — what board to get, and you'll hear the same answer. This is how that happened.

57.title: Gaming Boards Are Winning the Spec War, and Enthusiasts Are Paying Attention
57.lede: Hall-effect sensors and Rapid Trigger have done what RGB lighting and polling-rate marketing never could: closed the spec gap between gaming keyboards and enthusiast builds at the hardware layer. The divide persists in culture and community, but at the switch and firmware level, the lines are dissolving.

58.title: The o-ring mod: soft landings for tray-mount and top-mount boards
58.lede: A $2 bag of silicone O-rings is enough to give a tray-mount board meaningfully more flex and a cleaner sound. Here is the full procedure and what to realistically expect.

59.title: How optical switches actually sense a keypress
59.lede: An optical switch replaces the metal contact with a beam of light. That one change eliminates contact bounce entirely, reshapes the latency math, and is why some optical boards can offer per-key actuation at 0.1mm granularity. The mechanism is simpler than the marketing makes it sound.

60.title: Lubing switches: what to use, how much, and what to skip
60.lede: Four lubes, four application points, and one rule that prevents most mistakes: over-lubing is irreversible, under-lubing is not. Here is the practical reference.

61.title: The physics of thock: how every layer shapes your keyboard's sound
61.lede: Every component between your fingertip and the desk makes a decision about your keyboard's sound — the switch, the plate, the case, the surface it sits on. Understanding what each layer adds or subtracts is the difference between chasing a sound blindly and engineering it deliberately.

62.title: DCS Dolch closed at Divinikey — a computing-history colorway's first DCS-profile run
62.lede: The Dolch colorway — dark grey alphas, lighter grey mods, named after the 1990s portable workstations — ran a four-week DCS-profile group buy at Divinikey and nine regional storefronts, closing 2026-07-01.

63.title: Hall-effect keyboards: a practical buyer's guide
63.lede: Rapid trigger, per-key actuation depth, analog axis output — Hall-effect keyboards deliver all three, but only if the firmware matches the hardware. Here is what to look for, what to pay, and who should skip the category entirely.

64.title: Keyboard case materials, compared: aluminium, polycarbonate, and ABS
64.lede: The case is the largest resonant body in a keyboard. Aluminium, polycarbonate, and ABS each change the sound, feel, and weight profile in fundamentally different ways — here is what each material actually does.

65.title: Computex 2026: hall-effect keyboards enter the enthusiast conversation
65.lede: Computex 2026 (May 20–24) was the week hall-effect stopped being a gaming-peripheral curiosity and walked into the same room as enthusiast-grade chassis. Two boards made that argument concrete.

66.title: Stabilizers explained: from stock rattle to silent smoothness
66.lede: Stabilizers are the most acoustically influential component most builders treat as an afterthought. Understanding what they are and why they fail changes every build that follows.

67.title: DCS Grass Valley closes: what the profile's 2026 run tells us
67.lede: Grass Valley's group buy closed 2026-06-01 and the tracker dropped -18 that same week — but DCS Dolch opened the same day at +29. The momentum didn't dissipate; it transferred.

68.title: GMK CYL Ramune is the pastel pivot the CYL catalog needed
68.lede: GMK CYL Ramune opened on 2026-05-15 across ten regional vendors simultaneously — the broadest multi-vendor launch in the CYL sub-line's history. The pastel dual-blue and pink colorway is a deliberate break from the darker European-influenced palettes that have defined CYL since its first runs.

69.title: GMK CYL Selene closed at KBDfans with the sub-line's first material-first colorway
69.lede: GMK CYL Selene ran 2026-05-15 through 2026-06-19 at KBDfans with a special-effects glitter-reflect colorway in purple and teal over a silver-grey base. Designed by whysoda and inspired by the Greek Titaness of the Moon, the buy closed with Q1-Q2 2027 fulfillment ahead.

70.title: DCS Olivetti and the quiet rebellion against Cherry orthodoxy
70.lede: A March group buy closed strong, and eight weeks of steady tracker movement later, DCS Olivetti is the clearest sign that experienced builders are ready to argue about profile again.

71.title: Why the Drop Holy Panda X feels the way it does
71.lede: The Holy Panda was a six-month frankenswitch project for most of its life. The Drop Holy Panda X is the first version where the geometry, the spring tune, the housing pairing, and the factory lube were the spec — not the mod.

72.title: Spring swaps: what swapping the spring actually changes
72.lede: Swapping the spring is the most-discussed mod that does the least of what builders expect. Here is what the spring actually controls, what it does not, and when the swap is worth the afternoon.

73.title: Keychron's Q Ultra ZMK series brings 660h battery to the prebuilt-premium tier
73.lede: Keychron used CES 2026 to announce the Q Ultra line — five prebuilts (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q5, Q6) running ZMK rather than QMK/VIA. The 660h battery claim is the headline; the firmware swap is the actual story.

74.title: What Cherry's MX2A revision actually changed
74.lede: Cherry's MX2A landed in 2023 with a real engineering update — factory lube, tighter tolerances, the same 100M-press lifespan. The reason the discourse cooled isn't that the switch failed; it's that the enthusiast slot it aimed at was already claimed by the time it arrived.

75.title: GMK CYL Prussian Alert closed at KBDfans, capping the loudest GeekHack IC in the CYL sub-line's recent run
75.lede: GMK CYL Prussian Alert ran at KBDfans from 2026-05-15 through 2026-06-12 with a Bauhaus-leaning red-on-cream palette. The order window followed the loudest GMK CYL interest-check thread on GeekHack the sub-line had seen before an open.

76.title: GMK CYL Ishtar R2 closed at KBDfans with a second-and-likely-last shot at the lapis Mesopotamia palette
76.lede: GMK CYL Ishtar R2 ran 2026-04-17 through 2026-05-10 at KBDfans. The editorial event is not the open — it is the close. A second round on a Cherry-profile doubleshot ABS set is the second-and-likely-last shot at MSRP before the aftermarket takes over the palette.

77.title: How HMX took over the mid-tier linear slot
77.lede: Two years ago HMX was a name on a vendor page nobody pronounced confidently. In W19, the Cloud sat second among switches on our tracker and landed in half the $120 prebuilts the scene argues about. The rise wasn't an accident.

78.title: Why typing tests lie
78.lede: Monkeytype scores reward fast and forgiving. A daily driver needs comfortable and honest. Optimizing a build for the test selects for the wrong things — and the gap shows up around hour two, not in the leaderboard.

79.title: Plate materials, explained: what brass, FR4, POM, and aluminium actually change
79.lede: The plate is the cheapest variable in the build and the one builders argue about hardest. Most of the heat is misdirected — but a usable fraction of it is real, and the difference is worth pinning down.

80.title: GSK Sweet Nightmare ran a four-day window at KBDfans with an eight-variant matrix
80.lede: Goldenstar's Sweet Nightmare resin run opened at KBDfans on 2026-05-08 and closed 2026-05-11. The four-day window is unusually tight for a formal group buy, and the eight-variant matrix — four colorways across two finishes — compresses a configurator's worth of choices into a half-week.

81.title: Reading the Trends Tracker
81.lede: thock's Trends Tracker is a weekly snapshot of what is rising, falling, or holding flat across the hobby — switches, keycaps, layouts, vendors, and brands, scored on a single -100 to 100 scale and updated each Monday. This is what the columns mean and what they do not.

82.title: Pairing Oil Kings with the Mode Sonnet
82.lede: This pairing has been on the bench for months, and a free Sunday finally made it happen. The Sonnet is a soft 75 with a block mount, and Oil Kings are a heavy factory-lubed linear — together they hit a register worth coming back to.

83.title: Mode Sonnet R2 opened at CannonKeys
83.lede: Mode's second round of its 75% Sonnet board ran at CannonKeys from 2026-06-01 through 2026-07-15 after a vendor-side timeline shift. See the in-article update for the dates and accent-weight color options; the closed entry is archived at /group-buys/past.

84.title: The slow fade of Alice layouts
84.lede: Alice mounts had a clear moment between 2021 and 2023 — the splayed alphas, the angled bar, the promise of a typing posture that didn't twist your wrists. The thock trends snapshot for 2026-W19 pegs Alice movement at -18 and trending down. The layout still has loyal users, but the curve has bent.

85.title: When customs became vendor-first
85.lede: From 2018 through 2022 the typical custom shipped through one host vendor and a fan of regional proxies; by 2026 the baseline custom is a configurator on a vendor's own storefront. Boards moved. Keycap group buys mostly didn't.

86.title: Why the Gateron Oil King sounds the way it does
86.lede: Few stock linears earn the word 'creamy' on first press. The Oil King does, and the reason is not a secret stem material or a proprietary lube — it is a careful pairing of housing resins and a factory tune that other linears under thirty cents tend to skip.

87.title: Keycap profiles, compared: Cherry, OEM, SA, and MT3
87.lede: Most beginners agonize over switches for weeks, then drop any keycap set on top and discover the keycap was doing half the work all along. Profile shapes the sound, the typing angle, and the way a board reads on a desk — and the four profiles below cover almost every set on the market.

88.title: The split/ergo cohort grew up
88.lede: Split and ergonomic boards spent a decade as a hobbyist sub-cohort orbiting a stagger-majority. By 2026 the Voyager line, the Glove80, and a steady trickle of r/mk transition posts have pushed split/ergo across a visibility threshold — still a minority, but now a reference category instead of a footnote.

89.title: The tape mod: what one strip of Kapton actually does
89.lede: Three to five strips of painter's tape on the back of your PCB — that's the whole mod. The acoustic effect is real. Its magnitude depends almost entirely on the board underneath it.

90.title: GMK CYL GREG returns for round 2 at KBDfans
90.lede: Round 2 of GMK CYL GREG opened at KBDfans on 2026-05-01 and ran through 2026-05-29. The four-week window sits on the longer end for GMK CYL R2s, and the round-2 cadence itself is becoming the more interesting story as sets prove out in R1 and accumulate latent demand.

91.title: Lubing 101: what matters, what doesn't, and where to stop
91.lede: Lube moves the sound and feel of a switch in ways nothing else in the build can. It also chews up a Saturday and ruins switches when applied with the enthusiasm the rabbit-hole crowd recommends. Here is the version that earns its keep.

92.title: A beginner's guide to picking your first switch
92.lede: Switches are the single biggest factor in how a keyboard feels and sounds, and the catalog has grown overwhelming. This guide narrows the entire market into three families, explains who each one is for, and gives a three-step path from curiosity to a confident first purchase. By the end, the reader can pick a category without second-guessing.

93.title: Keyboard firmware, compared: QMK, VIA, and VIAL
93.lede: A first-time builder finishes a beautiful board, sits down to remap right-shift to enter, and discovers the firmware question is the one nobody warned them about. The catalog has three serious answers and an opinion about each.

94.title: GMK CYL King of the Seas opened at KBDfans in two colorways at once
94.lede: MiKeyDigit's nautical doubleshot ABS set opened at KBDfans on 2026-04-28 and ran through 2026-05-31. The rarer angle is the two-colorway split — The Sovereign in deep ocean blues and The Mutation in electric pink, sold concurrently inside the same buy rather than staggered as separate runs.

95.title: Sound dampening, compared: case foam, plate foam, PE foam, and the tape mod
95.lede: Four layers, four very different jobs. Here is what each sound mod actually changes, where it sits in the build stack, and the order to stack them in if you only have time for one or two.

96.title: How 'thock' became an acoustic spec, not an accident
96.lede: A decade ago a thocky board was the win condition of a $300 custom — the payoff for the right switches, the right lube job, the right patience. In 2026 the same sound is table-stakes for a $150 prebuilt: factory-lubed switches, silicone dampening, gasket-mounted plates, PBT doubleshot. The stack that used to be enthusiast-only is now what mid-tier vendors design toward from day one.

97.title: Mounting styles, compared: gasket, top-mount, tray, and integrated plate
97.lede: A builder who has lubed switches and tuned stabilizers and chosen a keycap profile and still cannot place why their next board feels different from their last one is usually meeting the mount style. The plate's relationship to the case is the half of the typing feel that nobody discusses on a sound test.

98.title: How 75 percent became the default custom layout
98.lede: Two years ago a custom-board recommendation defaulted to 65% with a polite note about 75% as the next step up. The KBD75 v3's staying power as a default recommendation, the QK75, and a crowded mid-tier have flipped that order. 75% is now the layout customs reach for first.

99.title: The PE foam mod: the two-dollar upgrade that actually works
99.lede: PE foam is one of the most accessible mods in the hobby — a $2 sheet between your PCB and case can noticeably reduce hollow resonance. Here is what it actually does, when to use it, and when to skip it.

100.title: Keycap materials, compared: ABS, PBT, and the rest
100.lede: Most builders obsess over switches and quietly accept whatever keycaps came in the box, then wonder six months in why their board doesn't sound like the YouTube video. Half the answer is the plastic. Material decides how a cap rings, how it ages, and what it feels like under a fingertip on day one and day one thousand.

101.title: How Hall-effect quietly became the new mid-premium default
101.lede: The polling-rate hype is loud and easy to wave off — 8K, 32K, numbers chasing each other up the spec sheet. The quieter story is that the magnetic-switch tier has stopped being a Wooting-shaped niche and has settled into the $100–$230 prebuilt slot the scene actually buys from. The volume has moved, not just the marketing.

102.title: Switch housings, compared: nylon, polycarbonate, POM, and the rest
102.lede: The housing line on a switch spec sheet is the second-most-important thing about a switch, after the type, and most buyers skim past it. Material decides how the switch rings, how the stem rails feel under a finger, and how much grace it gives a bad lube job. A 'PC top, nylon bottom' tag is doing more work than its three words suggest.

103.title: Stabilizer servicing: the one step most builders skip
103.lede: Most builders lube their switches meticulously and treat stabilizers as an afterthought. The rattle that survives a full stab lube job almost always traces back to one overlooked contact point.

104.title: What gasket mount actually delivers (and what it doesn't)
104.lede: The label appears on keyboards at every price point, from $90 prebuilts to $350 group-buy customs, but two boards with identical spec-sheet language can sound nothing alike. Here is what the term actually tells you, and what it doesn't.

105.title: Why clicky switches still have a constituency
105.lede: Linears and tactiles dominate the modern build conversation, and clickies barely appear in it. The reason is not that clicky switches have aged out — it is that the people who want them really want them, and the manufacturers know it.

106.title: The Nyawice puts a leaf-spring F1 mount under a friction-fit-cat-ears Alice
106.lede: An Alice-layout board with a leaf-spring F1 mount, a 9-degree typing angle, and four colorways of friction-fit silicone cat ears ran at CannonKeys through 2026-05-17. The mount type is the editorial story; the cat ears are the conversation.

107.title: How Topre's electrocapacitive switches actually work
107.lede: Topre is not just another switch — it is a third sensing lineage, parallel to the MX-style contact switches and the Hall-effect newcomers. Understanding why HHKB and Realforce typists pay what they pay starts with the fact that a Topre keypress does not close a circuit at all.

108.title: ZMK is becoming the wireless default for premium prebuilts
108.lede: A five-board flagship lineup running ZMK isn't a niche move; it's a market signal that an open-source firmware that lived in DIY-wireless territory for half a decade has crossed into mainstream-prebuilt anchor status. The vendor side has finally caught up with where the cohort already was.

109.title: How Hall-effect switches actually sense a keypress
109.lede: A Hall-effect switch is not a faster MX switch. It is a different sensing lineage — a magnet in the stem, a sensor on the PCB, and an analog voltage where contact closure used to be. The features the marketing pages lead with all unwind from that one architectural fact.

110.title: Switch films: do they actually do anything?
110.lede: Thin POM shims between your switch housings cost five dollars and promise a tighter, better-sounding switch. The mechanism is real. Whether it matters on your specific switches is a separate question.

documents.title: Four Switches, One Mechanism: What Stem Geometry Actually Changes
documents.lede: The Durock T1, the Boba U4T, the Holy Panda X, and the Gateron Lanes have spent four separate deep-dives citing each other as comparison points. None of those pieces stopped to say the obvious thing: all four generate their bump the same way. The leg geometry is the whole story.

documents.title: Artisan keycaps: a practical buying guide
documents.lede: A single sculpted cap on the Escape key can cost more than the switches underneath it, and the buying process looks nothing like ordering a keycap set. Here is what an artisan actually is, how the raffles work, and the one check that keeps a buyer from winning a cap their board can't use.

documents.title: GMK CYL Zombie's group buy, open through October 31, is already thock's steepest Halloween climb
documents.lede: GMK CYL Zombie, a Halloween-themed colorway running jointly through KBDfans and KeyAtlas from October 2 through October 31, 2026, has climbed to a score of 70 on thock's 2026-W42 trends tracker off an eight-week spark trail that hasn't flattened once. The buy is roughly a third of the way through its run, not winding down.

documents.title: Build of the week: the Drop CTRL goes synthwave under GMK Laser and Ink V2 Yellow
documents.lede: A board tuned for directness, a switch tuned for speed, and a keycap set tuned for attention — the gap between the first two and the third is the entire reason this build works.

documents.title: What a switch's gram number actually tells you before you buy
documents.lede: Every switch spec sheet carries two gram numbers — actuation and bottom-out — and treating them as one number is the most common mistake in a first switch purchase. Here's what each one measures, what ranges actually suit typing versus gaming, and why the same number can feel completely different depending on switch type.

documents.title: TMR is closing the gap on Hall-effect. It hasn't caught it.
documents.lede: TMR switches have climbed every week on thock's trend tracker from W38 through W42 — 55, 63, 71, 85, 90. That's the second-highest score on this week's board, and the gap behind Hall-effect's ceiling has gone from 42 points to 10 in five readings.

documents.title: What a TMR sensor is actually measuring under a magnetic switch
documents.lede: Keychron's Q16 HE 8K and Cherry's XTRFY TMR boards get covered as a new switch generation. The real change sits a few millimeters below the magnet — a tunnel junction reading field strength through resistance instead of voltage, with a noise floor low enough to matter at the shallow end of the stroke.

documents.title: Build of the week: the Bakeneko65 stops being a budget board under GMK Bentō R2 and Tecsee Sapphire V2
documents.lede: A $150 evergreen hotswap board, a sold-out doubleshot ABS set, and a sparkly polycarbonate tactile aren't a mismatch — the cheap part of this build is the entry price, not the result.

documents.title: Hardware caught up to Wooting. Firmware hasn't.
documents.lede: Wooting's 80HE+ preorder is the top mover on thock's 2026-W39 trends tracker, climbing from a score of 40 to 80 over eight weeks. The switch hardware behind it isn't the reason — Hall-effect sensing is table stakes across the category by September 2026. The firmware behind it still isn't matched.

documents.title: Wooting's 80HE+ preorder starts shipping in two waves this fall
documents.lede: Preorders for Wooting's 80HE+ opened September 17, 2026, and the first units are headed out the door in two separate waves — ABS and Module boards in late October, the zinc case and Lekker Knob Large accessory in mid-December.

documents.title: PCB flex cuts, explained: a flex budget milled straight into the board
documents.lede: No plate change, no gasket, no case redesign — just a slot routed through the fiberglass near a switch hole. Flex cuts are the cheapest lever a designer has for adding give to a board that otherwise has none, and the cheapness is exactly why they show up where they do.

documents.title: Wireless keyboard buying guide: Bluetooth, 2.4GHz, and the latency that actually matters
documents.lede: "Wireless" on a spec sheet hides three different radios with three different latency numbers, battery habits, and ways to lose the thing. Here's how to pick the one that matches an actual desk instead of a marketing slide.

documents.title: GMK CYL Red Devils is back after six years — and it's climbing the tracker faster than most first runs
documents.lede: GMK CYL Red Devils returns after six years for a second run, open Sept 14–Oct 10, 2026 via Omnitype and Keebz N Cables. The thock trends tracker has it up to a score of 68 off one of the steepest eight-week climbs of the season — and the buyer base behind that climb looks nothing like the one that bought the original.

documents.title: Keychron launches Q16 HE 8K with ceramic-TMR magnetic switches
documents.lede: Keychron's Q-series just picked up a Kickstarter campaign, a ceramic-housed TMR magnetic switch, and an 8000Hz polling claim in one launch. It's the brand's first bet on tunnel-magnetoresistance sensing rather than the Hall-effect tech it already made the category default.

documents.title: Build of the week: the mission control desk, in Class80, Godspeed, and Box White
documents.lede: A retro TKL, a steel-blue-and-cream SA set, and a clicky box-stem switch aren't three separate purchases here — they're one decision, made three times, that only works because each part solves a problem the other two create.

documents.title: How to clean and maintain a mechanical keyboard
documents.lede: Dust, oil, and crumbs collect on every keyboard whether anyone notices or not. A light routine on a fixed cadence keeps a board feeling and sounding like day one — no teardown required.

documents.title: Rapid trigger is a firmware algorithm, not a switch spec
documents.lede: A rapid-trigger switch is not a special switch. It is an ordinary analog sensor wired to a polling loop that redraws its own actuation point every cycle — and that loop, not the sensor, is where the real engineering happens.

documents.title: Cherry's tracker slide continues. Keychron's Kickstarter delivered.
documents.lede: Three weeks ago thock closed a piece with two open questions: would Cherry's brand line keep closing the gap toward positive territory, and would Keychron's V6 Ultra HE Kickstarter give the tracker something new to climb on. Both questions have answers now, and they point in opposite directions for a related reason.

documents.title: Drop restocks /dev/tty, the 2017 set that built the MT3 profile
documents.lede: Drop's catalog listing for Matt3o's original MT3 /dev/tty set flipped to in-stock in late August 2026, returning the dye-sub PBT run that defined the profile.

documents.title: Parts pairing for a split build: two independent halves, two independent decisions
documents.lede: A split board is two keyboards that happen to share a keymap. Most builders still buy parts for it like it's one — matching switches, ordering a single sculpted keycap set, and never touching the left half's tuning differently from the right's.

documents.title: Keyboard layout sizes, compared: 60% to full-size, which fits your desk
documents.lede: 60%, 65%, 75%, TKL, full-size — the names read like a settled taxonomy, but each cut trades away a specific cluster of keys for a specific amount of desk space. Here's what a reader actually keeps and gives up at each size, and how a firmware layer changes the math.

documents.title: Gateron Magnetic Jade: the Hall-effect linear built to be argued about like a mechanical one
documents.lede: Pull a Magnetic Jade apart and the parts list reads like a mid-tier mechanical linear: polycarbonate top, nylon bottom, POM stem, factory lube. Where the leaf would be, there is a magnet. That one substitution explains the feel, the sound, and why it will not fit half the Hall-effect boards on the market.

documents.title: What a silent switch actually silences — and what it can't
documents.lede: Every keystroke lands twice — once on the floor, once on the ceiling. Cherry molds an elastomer pad onto the stem to catch both; Gazzew fits a silicone one. The undamped Boba U4T shows what either approach is buying — about 14 dB on one tester's meter — and what it costs in travel, rebound, and a bump with nowhere left to go.

documents.title: Why stabilizers rattle: the engineering behind a smooth stab
documents.lede: A stabilizer has to be loose enough to slide and tight enough to stay quiet, and those two requirements contradict each other at three separate interfaces. Every rattle, tick, and clunk on a spacebar is one of those interfaces losing the argument.

documents.title: ANSI, ISO, or JIS: a practical layout buying guide
documents.lede: Two boards can look nearly identical in a listing photo and still take entirely different keycap sets. Here's how to read Enter key shape, bottom-row widths, and spec-sheet shorthand before ordering — not after a set arrives that doesn't fit.

documents.title: GMK CYL Orange Alert opens at Divinikey, the second Alert-series set to reach group buy this year
documents.lede: GMK CYL Orange Alert opened August 14 and runs through September 14, 2026, hosted by Divinikey with KBDfans, UniKeys, and Keebz N Cables running alongside — an orange-beige-gray Cherry-profile doubleshot set with Katakana accent legends and an estimated February 2027 ship.

documents.title: Hall-effect stopped climbing. That's not the same as cooling off.
documents.lede: The Hall Effect/Rapid Trigger category has held flat at 97 on thock's trends tracker for two straight weeks, after climbing from 82 in late June. A flat line at the top of the chart looks like fading interest if you're reading it as a stock ticker. Read as a market snapshot, it says something closer to the opposite.

documents.title: Hot-swap sockets: what you actually give up for the convenience
documents.lede: Tool-free switch swapping turned hot-swap PCBs into the default spec across the hobby, and the default is earned. Here is the honest, specific list of what a socket costs against a soldered joint — and the two cases where soldering is still the right call.

documents.title: Wuque Studio's summer update, and the Ikki68 Aurora holdover
documents.lede: A July 26 product-update post from Wuque Studio sent buyers back to the Ikki68 Aurora's listing page. Mammoth V2 and Promise V2 remain forum speculation, and no group buy has opened.

documents.title: How keycaps are actually made: double-shot, dye-sub, and the processes in between
documents.lede: Material and profile get the attention. The mold, the second shot, the transfer press, and the shrinkage table are what set the price, the lead time, and whether the legend is still there in ten years.

documents.title: GMK Just Beachy's group buy opens August 18 across five vendors on five regions
documents.lede: GMK Just Beachy opens for orders August 18, 2026 at five vendors spanning five regions at once — Keebz N Cables, Divinikey, Prototypist, KBDfans, and Unikeys — capping an eight-week climb on thock's Trends Tracker that hasn't logged a single down week.

documents.title: Leaf-spring mounts, explained: what a bending metal tab does that a foam strip cannot
documents.lede: The Nyawice's spec line and Mode's plate-tab mounting blocks both lean on one old idea — let a thin tab bend instead of a foam strip squash. The physics is textbook; the keyboard implementations are not, and the name covers more than one mechanism.

documents.title: GMK CYL TA Neo's group buy is closed — here's what a November 2026 ship estimate actually means
documents.lede: GMK CYL TA Neo closed its group buy July 17, 2026 after a June 19 open, and the thock trends tracker has logged two straight weeks of cooling attention since. That's not a warning sign — it's what every closed keycap buy looks like while it waits on production.

documents.title: What a split keyboard actually changes: the mechanics
documents.lede: A conventional keyboard bends the wrist three separate ways, and every ergonomic geometry on the market is a fix for exactly one of them. Sorting out which fix does what — and which claims the research backs — is the difference between buying a posture and buying a story.

documents.title: The Holee mod: what foam inside the switch actually buys you
documents.lede: Small pads of polyurethane foam cut and wedged inside the switch housing itself — not under the PCB, not behind it, not under the keycap. The Holee mod works at a smaller scale than every other foam mod in the hobby, and it costs proportionally more time.

documents.title: How the 60% became the default custom-keyboard layout
documents.lede: Every custom-keyboard buyer's guide since the mid-2010s opens with the same four-term vocabulary — 60%, 65%, 75%, TKL — as though it always existed. It didn't. One open-source PCB out of a geekhack thread is most of the reason that taxonomy exists at all.

documents.title: The Boba Family: One Housing Blend, Five Switches, and the Sound thock Is Named For
documents.lede: Gazzew designs, Outemu molds, and a plastic softer than nylon does the rest. Every Boba is the same chamber with something deliberately left out — and the pattern of subtractions is the whole family tree.

documents.title: How buckling-spring switches actually work
documents.lede: thock has already reached for the buckling-spring snap twice — once to describe a Topre dome, once to describe a click-bar's sharpness — without ever explaining what a buckling spring actually is. The mechanism predates both, and it is stranger and more mechanically honest than either.

documents.title: ZMK for wireless and split builds: a practical guide
documents.lede: QMK answers almost every firmware question on a wired board. Add a battery and a second half, and the honest answer changes — this is the guide for the builder standing at that fork.

documents.title: Mixing keycap profiles on one board: what actually works
documents.lede: Mixing profiles reads as a deliberate design choice or a rookie mistake depending entirely on where the swap lands. A handful of zones tolerate it well. The alpha block almost never does.

documents.title: Prototypist and the multi-project vendor model
documents.lede: Prototypist rarely carries just one thing at a time. The UK vendor's tracker signal has spent 2026 rising and falling with how many group buys it's running at once — and in July 2026 it's climbing again on the strength of its own pipeline rather than someone else's.

documents.title: Keyboard cables, compared: coiled, straight, and the connector that actually matters
documents.lede: Every builder eventually stares at a cable dropdown and has to decide whether to care. Here's what coiled versus straight actually changes, and why the keyboard-side connector — not the color of the sleeve — is the decision that follows the board for its whole life.

documents.title: OpenAI's first hardware is a Work Louder macro pad
documents.lede: Codex Micro, OpenAI's first piece of branded hardware, is a macro pad built by boutique vendor Work Louder on the bones of its $199 Creator Micro 2. It launched July 15, 2026 at $230, sold out within 24 hours, and now resells for $700-800+.

documents.title: Cherry bets on magnetic: the XTRFY pivot
documents.lede: Cherry's mainline MX switches have spent the better part of a year losing ground on the tracker. On July 3, 2026, Cherry's gaming sub-brand XTRFY answered not with another MX revision but with a magnetic-sensing switch — and gave the parent brand its first positive tracker signal in months.

documents.title: The Blaine V2: SE puts three mount systems in one kit and asks the buyer to pick
documents.lede: CannonKeys's F12 TKL follow-up ships with top mount, single-sided gasket, and o-ring hardware in the same box, plus a carbon-fiber bottom plate and a POM underside element it calls Volcano. The mount menu is the story.

documents.title: Nova Socket: Keychron's bet on not choosing a switch technology
documents.lede: A single hot-swap socket that accepts a standard mechanical switch or a TMR magnetic switch, decided per key, is a strange thing for a mainstream prebuilt brand to ship. It's also exactly the move Keychron has been building toward all year.

documents.title: The brass weight mod: what added mass actually buys you
documents.lede: Bolting a half-pound of brass into the bottom of a case is one of the more expensive mods in the hobby for how little it visibly does. It changes how a board sounds and sits on a desk — just not in the ways the marketing copy implies.

documents.title: Why the Durock T1's Bump Feels the Way It Does
documents.lede: The Durock T1 keeps turning up as the comparison point in other switches' deep-dives — the reference a reviewer reaches for when a bump needs to read as heavy and serious. It has never had its own.

documents.title: Why the Gazzew Boba U4T Rings Where the Boba U4 Stays Quiet
documents.lede: Same housing, same bump position — the U4T's whole personality comes down to what Gazzew left out. Pull the dampening pads from a Boba U4 and the bottom-out stops being polite.

documents.title: Choosing your first custom keyboard kit: a buyer's guide
documents.lede: Most first custom keyboards aren't built from loose parts and aren't bought finished — they're a barebones kit, a case-plate-PCB bundle that leaves the rest of the decision to the buyer. Here's how to make that decision without guessing.

documents.title: GMK CYL OG Extensions climbed eight interest-check weeks, then opened a group buy of its own
documents.lede: An interest check posted on Geekhack pulled ahead of both open GMK CYL group buys on the thock trends tracker — eight straight weekly reads without a single flat week — before opening a group buy of its own that has kept climbing since.

documents.title: Retrobrighting: what UV and peroxide actually reverse in yellowed ABS
documents.lede: Vintage ABS keycaps go the color of weak tea, and the hobby's fix is a jar of hair developer and a sunny windowsill. The chemistry behind that fix is real — but it reverses one specific kind of damage, and builders regularly aim it at problems it cannot touch.

documents.title: GMK CYL Masterpiece R2 closed at KBDfans, finishing the Katakana argument R1 started
documents.lede: Energieschleuder's six-year-later return to Japanese craftsmanship aesthetics climbed the thock tracker all window, scoring 46 in W26 before the buy closed June 26.

documents.title: GMK CYL Pandemonium: the eclipse-themed keycap set that closed on a plateau
documents.lede: DeltaKeyCo's Berserk eclipse group buy climbed the tracker from its June 1 open, posting a score of 33 in W26 with a flat direction — a mid-window plateau it held through its July 1 close.

documents.title: Split and ergonomic keyboards: a buyer's guide
documents.lede: Split doesn't automatically mean ergonomic, and ergonomic doesn't automatically mean split. Before spending money on either, a reader needs to know which of four separate design choices they're actually buying — and which one of them is solving their problem.

documents.title: Gateron Lanes: The Alps-Inspired Tactile Taking Over the Mid-Range
documents.lede: Gateron's Lanes draws its DNA from the Alps SKCM Orange — one of the most loved tactile mechanisms of the 1980s — and arrived in June 2026 with enough community conviction to sell out on first drop.

documents.title: Keychron's Quiet Takeover: How One Brand Became the Mechanical Keyboard Default
documents.lede: Ask almost anyone — a forum regular, a YouTube comment section, a Discord server for people who just bought their first mechanical keyboard — what board to get, and you'll hear the same answer. This is how that happened.

documents.title: Gaming Boards Are Winning the Spec War, and Enthusiasts Are Paying Attention
documents.lede: Hall-effect sensors and Rapid Trigger have done what RGB lighting and polling-rate marketing never could: closed the spec gap between gaming keyboards and enthusiast builds at the hardware layer. The divide persists in culture and community, but at the switch and firmware level, the lines are dissolving.

documents.title: The o-ring mod: soft landings for tray-mount and top-mount boards
documents.lede: A $2 bag of silicone O-rings is enough to give a tray-mount board meaningfully more flex and a cleaner sound. Here is the full procedure and what to realistically expect.

documents.title: How optical switches actually sense a keypress
documents.lede: An optical switch replaces the metal contact with a beam of light. That one change eliminates contact bounce entirely, reshapes the latency math, and is why some optical boards can offer per-key actuation at 0.1mm granularity. The mechanism is simpler than the marketing makes it sound.

documents.title: Lubing switches: what to use, how much, and what to skip
documents.lede: Four lubes, four application points, and one rule that prevents most mistakes: over-lubing is irreversible, under-lubing is not. Here is the practical reference.

documents.title: The physics of thock: how every layer shapes your keyboard's sound
documents.lede: Every component between your fingertip and the desk makes a decision about your keyboard's sound — the switch, the plate, the case, the surface it sits on. Understanding what each layer adds or subtracts is the difference between chasing a sound blindly and engineering it deliberately.

documents.title: DCS Dolch closed at Divinikey — a computing-history colorway's first DCS-profile run
documents.lede: The Dolch colorway — dark grey alphas, lighter grey mods, named after the 1990s portable workstations — ran a four-week DCS-profile group buy at Divinikey and nine regional storefronts, closing 2026-07-01.

documents.title: Hall-effect keyboards: a practical buyer's guide
documents.lede: Rapid trigger, per-key actuation depth, analog axis output — Hall-effect keyboards deliver all three, but only if the firmware matches the hardware. Here is what to look for, what to pay, and who should skip the category entirely.

documents.title: Keyboard case materials, compared: aluminium, polycarbonate, and ABS
documents.lede: The case is the largest resonant body in a keyboard. Aluminium, polycarbonate, and ABS each change the sound, feel, and weight profile in fundamentally different ways — here is what each material actually does.

documents.title: Computex 2026: hall-effect keyboards enter the enthusiast conversation
documents.lede: Computex 2026 (May 20–24) was the week hall-effect stopped being a gaming-peripheral curiosity and walked into the same room as enthusiast-grade chassis. Two boards made that argument concrete.

documents.title: Stabilizers explained: from stock rattle to silent smoothness
documents.lede: Stabilizers are the most acoustically influential component most builders treat as an afterthought. Understanding what they are and why they fail changes every build that follows.

documents.title: DCS Grass Valley closes: what the profile's 2026 run tells us
documents.lede: Grass Valley's group buy closed 2026-06-01 and the tracker dropped -18 that same week — but DCS Dolch opened the same day at +29. The momentum didn't dissipate; it transferred.

documents.title: GMK CYL Ramune is the pastel pivot the CYL catalog needed
documents.lede: GMK CYL Ramune opened on 2026-05-15 across ten regional vendors simultaneously — the broadest multi-vendor launch in the CYL sub-line's history. The pastel dual-blue and pink colorway is a deliberate break from the darker European-influenced palettes that have defined CYL since its first runs.

documents.title: GMK CYL Selene closed at KBDfans with the sub-line's first material-first colorway
documents.lede: GMK CYL Selene ran 2026-05-15 through 2026-06-19 at KBDfans with a special-effects glitter-reflect colorway in purple and teal over a silver-grey base. Designed by whysoda and inspired by the Greek Titaness of the Moon, the buy closed with Q1-Q2 2027 fulfillment ahead.

documents.title: DCS Olivetti and the quiet rebellion against Cherry orthodoxy
documents.lede: A March group buy closed strong, and eight weeks of steady tracker movement later, DCS Olivetti is the clearest sign that experienced builders are ready to argue about profile again.

documents.title: Why the Drop Holy Panda X feels the way it does
documents.lede: The Holy Panda was a six-month frankenswitch project for most of its life. The Drop Holy Panda X is the first version where the geometry, the spring tune, the housing pairing, and the factory lube were the spec — not the mod.

documents.title: Spring swaps: what swapping the spring actually changes
documents.lede: Swapping the spring is the most-discussed mod that does the least of what builders expect. Here is what the spring actually controls, what it does not, and when the swap is worth the afternoon.

documents.title: Keychron's Q Ultra ZMK series brings 660h battery to the prebuilt-premium tier
documents.lede: Keychron used CES 2026 to announce the Q Ultra line — five prebuilts (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q5, Q6) running ZMK rather than QMK/VIA. The 660h battery claim is the headline; the firmware swap is the actual story.

documents.title: What Cherry's MX2A revision actually changed
documents.lede: Cherry's MX2A landed in 2023 with a real engineering update — factory lube, tighter tolerances, the same 100M-press lifespan. The reason the discourse cooled isn't that the switch failed; it's that the enthusiast slot it aimed at was already claimed by the time it arrived.

documents.title: GMK CYL Prussian Alert closed at KBDfans, capping the loudest GeekHack IC in the CYL sub-line's recent run
documents.lede: GMK CYL Prussian Alert ran at KBDfans from 2026-05-15 through 2026-06-12 with a Bauhaus-leaning red-on-cream palette. The order window followed the loudest GMK CYL interest-check thread on GeekHack the sub-line had seen before an open.

documents.title: GMK CYL Ishtar R2 closed at KBDfans with a second-and-likely-last shot at the lapis Mesopotamia palette
documents.lede: GMK CYL Ishtar R2 ran 2026-04-17 through 2026-05-10 at KBDfans. The editorial event is not the open — it is the close. A second round on a Cherry-profile doubleshot ABS set is the second-and-likely-last shot at MSRP before the aftermarket takes over the palette.

documents.title: How HMX took over the mid-tier linear slot
documents.lede: Two years ago HMX was a name on a vendor page nobody pronounced confidently. In W19, the Cloud sat second among switches on our tracker and landed in half the $120 prebuilts the scene argues about. The rise wasn't an accident.

documents.title: Why typing tests lie
documents.lede: Monkeytype scores reward fast and forgiving. A daily driver needs comfortable and honest. Optimizing a build for the test selects for the wrong things — and the gap shows up around hour two, not in the leaderboard.

documents.title: Plate materials, explained: what brass, FR4, POM, and aluminium actually change
documents.lede: The plate is the cheapest variable in the build and the one builders argue about hardest. Most of the heat is misdirected — but a usable fraction of it is real, and the difference is worth pinning down.

documents.title: GSK Sweet Nightmare ran a four-day window at KBDfans with an eight-variant matrix
documents.lede: Goldenstar's Sweet Nightmare resin run opened at KBDfans on 2026-05-08 and closed 2026-05-11. The four-day window is unusually tight for a formal group buy, and the eight-variant matrix — four colorways across two finishes — compresses a configurator's worth of choices into a half-week.

documents.title: Reading the Trends Tracker
documents.lede: thock's Trends Tracker is a weekly snapshot of what is rising, falling, or holding flat across the hobby — switches, keycaps, layouts, vendors, and brands, scored on a single -100 to 100 scale and updated each Monday. This is what the columns mean and what they do not.

documents.title: Pairing Oil Kings with the Mode Sonnet
documents.lede: This pairing has been on the bench for months, and a free Sunday finally made it happen. The Sonnet is a soft 75 with a block mount, and Oil Kings are a heavy factory-lubed linear — together they hit a register worth coming back to.

documents.title: Mode Sonnet R2 opened at CannonKeys
documents.lede: Mode's second round of its 75% Sonnet board ran at CannonKeys from 2026-06-01 through 2026-07-15 after a vendor-side timeline shift. See the in-article update for the dates and accent-weight color options; the closed entry is archived at /group-buys/past.

documents.title: The slow fade of Alice layouts
documents.lede: Alice mounts had a clear moment between 2021 and 2023 — the splayed alphas, the angled bar, the promise of a typing posture that didn't twist your wrists. The thock trends snapshot for 2026-W19 pegs Alice movement at -18 and trending down. The layout still has loyal users, but the curve has bent.

documents.title: When customs became vendor-first
documents.lede: From 2018 through 2022 the typical custom shipped through one host vendor and a fan of regional proxies; by 2026 the baseline custom is a configurator on a vendor's own storefront. Boards moved. Keycap group buys mostly didn't.

documents.title: Why the Gateron Oil King sounds the way it does
documents.lede: Few stock linears earn the word 'creamy' on first press. The Oil King does, and the reason is not a secret stem material or a proprietary lube — it is a careful pairing of housing resins and a factory tune that other linears under thirty cents tend to skip.

documents.title: Keycap profiles, compared: Cherry, OEM, SA, and MT3
documents.lede: Most beginners agonize over switches for weeks, then drop any keycap set on top and discover the keycap was doing half the work all along. Profile shapes the sound, the typing angle, and the way a board reads on a desk — and the four profiles below cover almost every set on the market.

documents.title: The split/ergo cohort grew up
documents.lede: Split and ergonomic boards spent a decade as a hobbyist sub-cohort orbiting a stagger-majority. By 2026 the Voyager line, the Glove80, and a steady trickle of r/mk transition posts have pushed split/ergo across a visibility threshold — still a minority, but now a reference category instead of a footnote.

documents.title: The tape mod: what one strip of Kapton actually does
documents.lede: Three to five strips of painter's tape on the back of your PCB — that's the whole mod. The acoustic effect is real. Its magnitude depends almost entirely on the board underneath it.

documents.title: GMK CYL GREG returns for round 2 at KBDfans
documents.lede: Round 2 of GMK CYL GREG opened at KBDfans on 2026-05-01 and ran through 2026-05-29. The four-week window sits on the longer end for GMK CYL R2s, and the round-2 cadence itself is becoming the more interesting story as sets prove out in R1 and accumulate latent demand.

documents.title: Lubing 101: what matters, what doesn't, and where to stop
documents.lede: Lube moves the sound and feel of a switch in ways nothing else in the build can. It also chews up a Saturday and ruins switches when applied with the enthusiasm the rabbit-hole crowd recommends. Here is the version that earns its keep.

documents.title: A beginner's guide to picking your first switch
documents.lede: Switches are the single biggest factor in how a keyboard feels and sounds, and the catalog has grown overwhelming. This guide narrows the entire market into three families, explains who each one is for, and gives a three-step path from curiosity to a confident first purchase. By the end, the reader can pick a category without second-guessing.

documents.title: Keyboard firmware, compared: QMK, VIA, and VIAL
documents.lede: A first-time builder finishes a beautiful board, sits down to remap right-shift to enter, and discovers the firmware question is the one nobody warned them about. The catalog has three serious answers and an opinion about each.

documents.title: GMK CYL King of the Seas opened at KBDfans in two colorways at once
documents.lede: MiKeyDigit's nautical doubleshot ABS set opened at KBDfans on 2026-04-28 and ran through 2026-05-31. The rarer angle is the two-colorway split — The Sovereign in deep ocean blues and The Mutation in electric pink, sold concurrently inside the same buy rather than staggered as separate runs.

documents.title: Sound dampening, compared: case foam, plate foam, PE foam, and the tape mod
documents.lede: Four layers, four very different jobs. Here is what each sound mod actually changes, where it sits in the build stack, and the order to stack them in if you only have time for one or two.

documents.title: How 'thock' became an acoustic spec, not an accident
documents.lede: A decade ago a thocky board was the win condition of a $300 custom — the payoff for the right switches, the right lube job, the right patience. In 2026 the same sound is table-stakes for a $150 prebuilt: factory-lubed switches, silicone dampening, gasket-mounted plates, PBT doubleshot. The stack that used to be enthusiast-only is now what mid-tier vendors design toward from day one.

documents.title: Mounting styles, compared: gasket, top-mount, tray, and integrated plate
documents.lede: A builder who has lubed switches and tuned stabilizers and chosen a keycap profile and still cannot place why their next board feels different from their last one is usually meeting the mount style. The plate's relationship to the case is the half of the typing feel that nobody discusses on a sound test.

documents.title: How 75 percent became the default custom layout
documents.lede: Two years ago a custom-board recommendation defaulted to 65% with a polite note about 75% as the next step up. The KBD75 v3's staying power as a default recommendation, the QK75, and a crowded mid-tier have flipped that order. 75% is now the layout customs reach for first.

documents.title: The PE foam mod: the two-dollar upgrade that actually works
documents.lede: PE foam is one of the most accessible mods in the hobby — a $2 sheet between your PCB and case can noticeably reduce hollow resonance. Here is what it actually does, when to use it, and when to skip it.

documents.title: Keycap materials, compared: ABS, PBT, and the rest
documents.lede: Most builders obsess over switches and quietly accept whatever keycaps came in the box, then wonder six months in why their board doesn't sound like the YouTube video. Half the answer is the plastic. Material decides how a cap rings, how it ages, and what it feels like under a fingertip on day one and day one thousand.

documents.title: How Hall-effect quietly became the new mid-premium default
documents.lede: The polling-rate hype is loud and easy to wave off — 8K, 32K, numbers chasing each other up the spec sheet. The quieter story is that the magnetic-switch tier has stopped being a Wooting-shaped niche and has settled into the $100–$230 prebuilt slot the scene actually buys from. The volume has moved, not just the marketing.

documents.title: Switch housings, compared: nylon, polycarbonate, POM, and the rest
documents.lede: The housing line on a switch spec sheet is the second-most-important thing about a switch, after the type, and most buyers skim past it. Material decides how the switch rings, how the stem rails feel under a finger, and how much grace it gives a bad lube job. A 'PC top, nylon bottom' tag is doing more work than its three words suggest.

documents.title: Stabilizer servicing: the one step most builders skip
documents.lede: Most builders lube their switches meticulously and treat stabilizers as an afterthought. The rattle that survives a full stab lube job almost always traces back to one overlooked contact point.

documents.title: What gasket mount actually delivers (and what it doesn't)
documents.lede: The label appears on keyboards at every price point, from $90 prebuilts to $350 group-buy customs, but two boards with identical spec-sheet language can sound nothing alike. Here is what the term actually tells you, and what it doesn't.

documents.title: Why clicky switches still have a constituency
documents.lede: Linears and tactiles dominate the modern build conversation, and clickies barely appear in it. The reason is not that clicky switches have aged out — it is that the people who want them really want them, and the manufacturers know it.

documents.title: The Nyawice puts a leaf-spring F1 mount under a friction-fit-cat-ears Alice
documents.lede: An Alice-layout board with a leaf-spring F1 mount, a 9-degree typing angle, and four colorways of friction-fit silicone cat ears ran at CannonKeys through 2026-05-17. The mount type is the editorial story; the cat ears are the conversation.

documents.title: How Topre's electrocapacitive switches actually work
documents.lede: Topre is not just another switch — it is a third sensing lineage, parallel to the MX-style contact switches and the Hall-effect newcomers. Understanding why HHKB and Realforce typists pay what they pay starts with the fact that a Topre keypress does not close a circuit at all.

documents.title: ZMK is becoming the wireless default for premium prebuilts
documents.lede: A five-board flagship lineup running ZMK isn't a niche move; it's a market signal that an open-source firmware that lived in DIY-wireless territory for half a decade has crossed into mainstream-prebuilt anchor status. The vendor side has finally caught up with where the cohort already was.

documents.title: How Hall-effect switches actually sense a keypress
documents.lede: A Hall-effect switch is not a faster MX switch. It is a different sensing lineage — a magnet in the stem, a sensor on the PCB, and an analog voltage where contact closure used to be. The features the marketing pages lead with all unwind from that one architectural fact.

documents.title: Switch films: do they actually do anything?
documents.lede: Thin POM shims between your switch housings cost five dollars and promise a tighter, better-sounding switch. The mechanism is real. Whether it matters on your specific switches is a separate question.
